newsitem.title: CHINA: Hopewell, Thailand jockey on project - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hopewell, Thailand jockey on project - analysts.

text.p: Hopewell Holdings Ltd and the Thai government appeared to be jockeying for position on Thursday in the on-going saga surrounding the construction of a transit system in Bangkok, analysts said.

In comments Hopewell said took the company completely by surprise, a Thai government official said Thailand could scrap Hopewell's contract to build and operate the multi-level rail and highway network if Hopewell failed to come up with a firm financing package by the end of July.
Hopewell responded it had not heard from the Thai government on Thursday and remained "very committed" to the project.
"It is possible it is one more step in the negotiating process," an analyst at a European brokerage firm said of the Thai government's comments. "It could be a tactic."
Hopewell said last Friday it was unable to complete the long-delayed mass transit system as planned because of adverse economic conditions in Thailand and the baht's recent de facto devaluation.
Hopewell said the baht's 15-20 percent depreciation since the currency's July 2 float meant international banks backing the scheme were "reassessing the project financing structure".

"If (Hopewell) cannot come up with a firm financing package by the end of July, the Communications Ministry can scrap the contract," Sathien Wongvichien, Thailand's deputy permanent secretary for transport and communications, said on Thursday.
Market sources said on Thursday Hopewell was seeking to raise funds through a bond issue.
Hopewell declined to comment.
An analyst at a Japanese brokerage firm said it would be "very, very hard" for Hopewell to raise financing but Thailand was keen to get the project in place.
"It is important to the Thai government's pride to have the BERTS (Bangkok Elevated Rail Train System) system running by the Asian Games," said analyst Geoffrey Cheng at CEF GC Brokerage.
The Games will be held in December 1998.
"I would say that certainly there is some risk of non-completion, more so now than before," the Japanese analyst said.
"But I don't think this is as final a statement as it appears to be. This verbal sparring has been going on for a long time now. Maybe it is escalating -- it seems to be heating up."
He said the Thai government was possibly trying to extract a firm commitment from Hopewell.
The Hong Kong company has been wrangling with successive Thai governments for a decade over the US$3.2 billion BERTS project, which is slated to be finished by 1999.
"Hopewell has faced seven different Thai governments in seven years," a Hopewell spokeswoman said.
The company has spent about US$560 million on the project.
Sathien said the Thai government would probably find new investors to carry on the long-delayed project, with Hopewell scaling down its role from project operator to its future shareholder.
"The project may be scaled back altogether. If Hopewell loses the project, from an accounting point of view they would have to take a massive writeoff.
"They would have to write off their investment unless they could sell the project to someone else," the analyst at the Japanese brokerage said.
"The bad news would be that they have very few projects going and the good news would be that at least they are getting rid of a bad project."
